extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in 19th-century Catholic missions, convent life, and Loretto sisterhood history
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the signs of vocation, internal rules, spiritual training, and procedural practices for the Loretto (Friends of Mary) sisterhood in early 19th-century Kentucky and its colonies. Includes indications of what the founder (Father Nerinckx) considered essential qualities, rites, and administrative rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of vocation to the institute
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted criterion: "An uncommon love for Jesus suffering and Mary sorrowing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That devotion is called the touchstone of a religious call to his sisterhood; it pervades all his labors and is constantly recalled to the sisters. Father Nerinckx places this as the first and most important sign of vocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventual observance for postulants and sisters
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulants and sisters are to observe the Mother-house rules: rise early, have prayers and meditation in common, keep silence, take their meals, and observe the recreation time "just like religious of long standing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical enforcement included teaching the rules to be learned by heart, giving instructions twice a day, strict silence (e.g., "you are not allowed to talk on the road"), and regular communal devotions. Father frequently instructed them and emphasized charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process for receiving postulants
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: candidates present themselves, are kindly received, handed a copy of the rules to learn by heart, and given instructions twice daily for a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postulants were formed into a little community immediately and expected to live under conventual rules from the start; examples show close pastoral oversight and examination of candidates (e.g., careful examination of reported visions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual training emphasis (penance and mortification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Father Nerinckx applied himself to 'imbue them thoroughly with the spirit of penance and mortification,' which he described as the groundwork of the whole fabric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To this end he jotted down notes for guidance and gave frequent oral instructions; this spiritual formation was treated as more important than institutional expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festival and devotional calendar practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Friday in Passion-week is designated 'the great festival in the Society of the Friends of Mary' as the day to commemorate the sorrows of the Blessed Lady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Friends of Mary at the Foot of the Cross they claim Passion-week Friday as their festive day. Father suggests the Passion of Our Lord 'might be read, in Holy Week, soon after dinner on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities exemplifying true piety
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative criteria of true piety: love of God that elevates and purifies natural affections rather than crushing them; firmness in vocation; fidelity to community obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Sister Alexandrina: innocence, industry, virtue, labor, prayer, fasting, seeking mortifications, never violating the rule of silence, never absent from community exercises, pleasant in demeanor, affectionate to parents but loving God more. These behaviors are presented as evidence of a genuine vocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for election of Superior-General
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedural rule: 'The rule regulating the election of a Superior-General provided that a new election should take place every three years.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in practice: the first regular election occurred about the Feast of the Purification and installation on March 25, 1822; lists of appointed Mother Superiors for various houses are provided as examples of governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical criteria for founding/colonizing new houses
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations respond to external requests (towns, bishops) but require suitable personnel and resources; Father noted the need for provision for obtaining or training teachers and adequate numbers of clergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colonies were sent with a superior and sisters (e.g., twelve sisters under Sister Joanna Miles). Foundations were arranged with local bishops/authorities; Father also cautioned that the society should make volunteers 'sensible of the kind of duty they may have to comply with' (e.g., service in hospital and orphanage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment suitability and labor expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sisters may be called to teach, run hospitals, orphanages, or do other charitable works; communities must be prepared to 'feed and clothe' members and face material scarcities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Father emphasized matching duties to volunteers' expectations and warned about limited financial resources (e.g., Loretto had barely one paying pupil). Practical labor (timber cutting, hauling) and participation in community manual work were expected; leadership sometimes sent sisters to assist other institutions when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of extraordinary claims (visions, vocations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Father Nerinckx conducted due investigation and careful examination into reported supernatural occurrences before accepting them as genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sister Alexandrina's vision was believed by Father only after careful examination; the text notes Father 'was no enthusiast' and judged such claims prudently.
